meta.title: A Cross-Task Analysis of Post-Training Quantization Robustness in Earth Observation
meta.authorsHtml: Franz Figueroa<sup>∗</sup><sup>1</sup>, César Cabezas<sup>1</sup>, Jose Carlos Salinas<sup>1</sup>, Gonzalo Alvis<sup>1</sup>

meta.venue: Proceedings of the 3rd Conference on AI in and for Space (SPAICE 2026)

abstract: Deploying deep neural networks onboard Earth Observation (EO) platforms requires model compression strategies that reduce memory footprint and computational cost without compromising task performance. Post-training quantization (PTQ) is a deployment-viable approach, yet its robustness across different EO task types remains insufficiently characterized. This work evaluates the algorithmic robustness of static INT8 PTQ across three EO tasks—scene-level classification, object-level detection, and pixel-level semantic segmentation—using a shared ResNet-50 backbone and backbone-only quantization as a controlled compression strategy. Evaluation is performed on EuroSAT, DIOR, and LoveDA, with model size reduction and compression ratio reported as hardware-agnostic efficiency indicators. Results show that quantization sensitivity differs across the evaluated EO task types: scene classification and semantic segmentation exhibit limited degradation under backbone-only INT8 PTQ, while object detection with Faster R-CNN shows substantially higher sensitivity at a reduced compression ratio. This behavior may be associated with error propagation across the two-stage pipeline, suggesting that architectural factors may contribute beyond spatial prediction granularity alone. These results provide a baseline for assessing the trade-offs of INT8 PTQ across EO task types in resource-constrained onboard systems.

blocks.html: Earth Observation (EO) systems are increasingly shifting from passive data acquisition toward higher levels of on-board autonomy, driven by the need for low-latency predictions and reduced dependence on downlink-limited ground processing [1, 2]. Modern missions demand not only image capture, but also onboard interpretation capabilities such as scene understanding, object localization, and dense land-cover mapping for prioritization and decision support [1, 3]. These capabilities rely on deep neural networks, which have demonstrated strong performance across classification, detection, and semantic segmentation tasks in computer vision and remote sensing applications [4, 5].

However, their deployment in space-constrained environments remains challenging due to strict size, weight, power, and reliability constraints, as well as the need for radiation tolerance and fault resilience in onboard computing platforms [1, 2, 6]. Model compression techniques, particularly low-precision inference, have therefore emerged as promising strategies to alleviate these constraints [4, 7].

Specifically, post-training quantization (PTQ) enables the reduction of numerical precision (e.g., FP32 to INT8) with limited or no retraining overhead, depending on the method and target architecture [7, 8]. In terrestrial image classification, INT8 quantization often preserves accuracy with relatively small degradation when appropriate calibration and quantization schemes are used, although the exact drop depends on architecture and configuration [7, 8]. Nevertheless, its behavior across tasks of increasing structural and spatial complexity remains insufficiently characterized, especially in the context of EO applications.

Existing quantization studies have largely emphasized image classification benchmarks and architectures, while unified cross-task analyses that jointly examine object detection and semantic segmentation remain less common, especially in EO settings [4, 7–9]. This matters because EO pipelines routinely use detection and segmentation tasks, for example in aerial object detection and in landuse/land-cover (LULC) semantic segmentation for geospatial mapping [3, 10, 11]. Furthermore, many deploymentoriented quantization studies report hardware-dependent metrics such as latency or throughput on specific accelerators, which is essential for deployment but makes it difficult to isolate task-related sensitivity from platform-specific implementation effects [9, 12]. It therefore remains an open question whether quantization-induced performance degradation differs across EO task types when evaluated as an algorithmic robustness property rather than a hardware-specific effect, and which task or architectural characteristics may contribute to this sensitivity.

In this work, we evaluate the algorithmic robustness of static INT8 post-training quantization across three EO tasks spanning different levels of spatial prediction: scene-level classification, object-level detection, and pixel-level semantic segmentation. We employ ResNet-50 as a shared convolutional backbone across all tasks to isolate quantization effects from architectural variability in the feature extractor, and apply backbone-only INT8 PTQ as a controlled and practically feasible quantization strategy. Evaluation is performed on established EO datasets spanning the three task categories: EuroSAT [13] for scene classification, DIOR [14] for object detection, and LoveDA [15] for semantic segmentation. We report task-specific performance metrics alongside hardware-agnostic efficiency indicators—model size reduction and compression ratio—to characterize the algorithmic impact of quantization independently of a specific deployment platform.
Our contributions are as follows:

1. A unified cross-task evaluation of static INT8 PTQ robustness across scene-, object-, and pixel-level EO tasks using a shared ResNet-50 backbone and backbone-only quantization as a controlled compression strategy. Results show substantial differences in quantization sensitivity across the evaluated task types: classification and segmentation exhibit limited degradation under INT8 PTQ, while two-stage object detection shows substantially higher sensitivity, which is consistent with error propagation across its sequential pipeline stages.

2. A hardware-agnostic characterization of quantization sensitivity across EO tasks, reported using model size reduction and compression ratio alongside task-specific performance metrics. This baseline highlights architectural pipeline depth as a potential factor influencing cross-task quantization sensitivity and motivates further evaluation of single-stage detectors to disentangle architectural effects from task-specific spatial requirements.

We evaluate quantization sensitivity across three Earth Observation tasks with different spatial prediction requirements: scene-level classification (global semantic labeling), object-level detection (instance localization and classification), and pixel-level semantic segmentation (dense perpixel labeling). These tasks range from global feature aggregation to localized instance prediction and dense spatial prediction.

We use ResNet-50 [16] as the common convolutional backbone across the three task configurations. ResNet-based architectures are widely adopted in Earth Observation applications, including remote sensing scene classification and object detection, due to their strong representation capability and generalization performance on high-resolution imagery [5, 17]. Moreover, ResNet-50 is commonly used as a reference backbone in quantization research and benchmarking studies [4, 18]. Its standard convolution–batch normalization–activation design aligns well with widely used quantization pipelines and facilitates reproducible evaluation of low-precision inference methods [19].

Task-specific heads comprise: global average pooling and a fully connected classifier for scene classification; Faster R-CNN [20] with Feature Pyramid Network (FPN) [21] for object detection; and DeepLabV3 [22] with Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (ASPP) and bilinear upsampling for semantic segmentation. The overall experimental workflow is summarized in Figure 1.

We adopt static INT8 post-training quantization (PTQ) without fine-tuning. PTQ is selected because it enables efficient model compression without retraining, making it suitable for deployment scenarios where full access to training data or computational resources is limited [4, 18, 19].

Weights are quantized using per-channel symmetric quantization, which better preserves filter-level dynamic range and reduces accuracy degradation in convolutional layers [19]. Activations are quantized using per-tensor affine quantization, a common configuration that balances numerical fidelity with hardware-efficient inference.

blocks.html: Calibration relies on Min-Max observers applied to representative training images to estimate activation ranges for quantization. Min-Max calibration is widely used in PTQ pipelines due to its simplicity and compatibility with graph-based quantization frameworks [19].
We evaluate quantization robustness on three Earth Observation datasets spanning increasing spatial granularity:
• EuroSAT (Scene classification): 27,000 Sentinel-2 RGB images (10 m GSD) covering 10 land-use classes, split into 80% training and 20% validation following the standard random partition [13].

• DIOR (Object detection): A large-scale aerial object detection benchmark containing 23,463 images at 800×800 pixels with 20 object categories and 192,472 annotated instances. The dataset is divided into 5,862 training, 5,863 validation, and 11,725 test images. We employ horizontal bounding box (HBB) annotations [14].

• LoveDA (Semantic segmentation): 5,987 high-resolution images (0.3 m GSD) for urban and rural land-cover mapping with 7 semantic classes (Back-ground, Building, Road, Water, Barren, Forest, Agriculture), divided into training (70%), validation (15%), and test (15%) sets [15]. Both rural and urban domains are included in training and evaluation.

All images are resized to 224 × 224 pixels for classification and 512 × 512 pixels for detection and segmentation, with standard ImageNet normalization applied (µ = [0.485, 0.456, 0.406], σ = [0.229, 0.224, 0.225]).

All models are implemented in PyTorch (2.10.0, CUDA 12.8) and trained to FP32 convergence on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 (8 GB VRAM) before quantization is applied. All parameters are explicitly initialized and maintained in torch.float32 throughout training. We use SGD with momentum 0.9, weight decay 10−4, and an initial learning rate of 10−2 with cosine annealing, training for 100 epochs (classification) or 50 epochs (detection and segmentation) with early stopping patience of 10 epochs. For detection, the learning rate is reduced to 10−3 to ensure stable convergence. Batch sizes are set to 64 (classification), 4 (detection), and 4 (segmentation).

Post-training quantization is performed using PyTorch’s FX Graph Mode pipeline without fine-tuning or quantization-aware training. Weights are quantized using per-channel symmetric quantization and activations using per-tensor affine quantization.

For calibration, we use 500 stratified training images per dataset to compute Min-Max ranges for activation quantization. For EuroSAT, stratification is performed by land-use class (50 images per class). For LoveDA, stratification is performed by domain (250 Rural and 250 Urban images). For DIOR, stratification is performed by object category (approximately 25 images per class).

INT8 quantization is applied exclusively to the ResNet- 50 backbone. This setup provides a controlled cross-task comparison by restricting quantization to the shared backbone and keeping task-specific heads in FP32, though the resulting compression ratio is inherently constrained by the parameter distribution between backbone and task-specific heads. To contextualize the scope of quantization across tasks, we introduce quantization coverage, defined as the fraction of total model parameters subject to INT8 quantization.

We report task-specific performance using top-1 accuracy (classification), mAP50 (detection), and mean Intersection over Union (segmentation). Segmentation masks use perpixel integer labels (classes 1–7), remapped to 0–6 prior to loss computation, with pixels outside this range assigned ignore_index = 255. where M denotes the corresponding task metric. We additionally report model size (MB) and compression ratio (SizeF P32/SizeINT8) as hardware-agnostic efficiency indicators.
Table 1 and Table 2 summarize the performance impact of backbone-only INT8 quantization and the resulting model compression across the three EO tasks.

Scene-level classification exhibits near-negligible sensitivity to INT8 backbone quantization (∆R = 0.07%), with a 4× compression ratio and a quantization coverage of 99.5%. The near-identical FP32 and INT8 accuracy scores suggest that global semantic representations are largely insensitive to 8-bit discretization of backbone features.

blocks.html: Semantic segmentation exhibits a more noticeable, yet still limited, performance decrease (∆R = 1.19%) at 1.7× compression ratio and 55.8% quantization coverage. While this drop is greater than that observed in scene classification, the overall degradation remains marginal.

Object detection exhibits substantially higher degradation (∆R = 38.28%) under the same backbone-only quantization configuration, alongside a reduced compression ratio of 1.9× and a quantization coverage of 64.6%. The magnitude of the performance drop is disproportionate relative to both the quantization scope—which remains restricted to the shared backbone—and the degradation observed in the other two tasks, suggesting that factors beyond spatial prediction granularity may influence detection sensitivity. Notably, detection presents a lower quantization coverage than classification (64.6% vs. 99.5%), yet the observed degradation is orders of magnitude larger.

The results show that quantization sensitivity differs across the evaluated Earth Observation (EO) task types, with the largest degradation observed for object detection. Scene-level classification remains largely unaffected by backbone quantization, while semantic segmentation exhibits modest degradation. In contrast, object detection demonstrates substantially higher sensitivity under the same quantization configuration.

However, the detection results reveal an important nuance: the observed sensitivity cannot be explained by spatial prediction granularity alone. Architectural pipeline structure may also contribute to the observed sensitivity. In two-stage detectors such as Faster R-CNN, backbone features influence both region proposal generation and final classification, creating a sequential dependency between intermediate predictions. Under this structure, quantization-induced perturbations in backbone feature maps may propagate across multiple pipeline stages, potentially amplifying their impact on the final output. The observed dissociation between quantization coverage and performance impact—where detection shows the highest sensitivity despite a quantization coverage comparable to segmentation—is consistent with the possibility that architectural factors contribute to detection sensitivity beyond the magnitude of numerical precision reduction alone.

This architectural difference may help explain why quantization-induced perturbations have a smaller observed impact on the final prediction in the evaluated classification and segmentation models. In classification models, the backbone representation is directly aggregated into a single global prediction, while segmentation models rely on dense spatial decoding but maintain a single-stage inference structure.

From a deployment perspective, these findings highlight important differences in the quantizability of EO inference pipelines. Classification and segmentation models demonstrate strong compatibility with static INT8 posttraining quantization, achieving model compression with minimal impact on predictive performance. These characteristics make them attractive candidates for deployment in resource-constrained onboard computing environments, where memory footprint and energy efficiency are critical design constraints.

Detection models, however, present a more complex trade-off between compression efficiency and prediction reliability. The present study is limited to post-training quantization and does not evaluate quantization-aware training (QAT), which could be investigated as a potential strategy to mitigate the observed degradation. Other approaches, such as partial quantization or mixed-precision inference, could likewise be explored to preserve detection accuracy while maintaining meaningful model compression.

Overall, the findings suggest that both task characteristics and architectural pipeline design may contribute to quantization sensitivity. However, the current experimental setup does not permit full disentanglement of these factors: the higher sensitivity observed in detection may be associated with both the spatial precision demands of instance localization and the sequential structure of Faster R-CNN, but their individual contributions cannot be isolated without evaluating alternative detection architectures under equivalent conditions.

This work evaluated the robustness of static INT8 posttraining quantization across three Earth Observation tasks using a shared ResNet-50 backbone, characterizing quantization sensitivity as an algorithmic property of task type and architectural pipeline design rather than a hardware-specific effect.

The results indicate that static INT8 PTQ can provide substantial compression with minimal performance degradation for the evaluated classification and segmentation models, while the evaluated Faster R-CNN detection model exhibits substantial sensitivity to backbone-only quantization. These results highlight the need to consider task-specific quantization sensitivity when evaluating models for resource-constrained EO deployment.

Future work should extend the evaluation to multiple detection and backbone architectures, including singlestage detectors, to better disentangle task and architectural effects. Further evaluation of lower-precision regimes and quantization-aware training could then assess alternative strategies for detection-critical applications.
